summary:
Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. The 2020 Rules under the Act added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had already directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those statutory protections sit under an active constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, delivering a reserved verdict across 12 shariat petitions, ruled that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The struck sections remained in force pending appeals, and the UK Home Office country-policy note of November 2025 records that transgender and intersex people remain protected under the 2018 Act while describing the 2023 declaration and the litigation around it as unresolved.

Amnesty International responded to the verdict on 19 May 2023 as a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group, and had warned the government two days earlier not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards. A further retrograde proposal surfaced later: Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has put forward a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity, an active legislative push against self-identification.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range in Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. In February 2026 reporting, activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana survived three bullets fired through a Karachi door at night, and the account describes a wave of violence that has left transgender Pakistanis afraid to go out.

Custody and police handling are a specific danger. Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief finds that the 2018 Act's advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice, and identifies implementation failure rather than absence of law as the central problem, with recommendations directed at custody and police safeguards. Local reporting from October 2025 documents the same gap at street level: rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals, street harassment, and suspicion or ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is a documented failure point. In 2016 the 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or the women's ward; men in the hospital taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. Some transgender women administer hormones and silicone under unsupervised and unhygienic conditions because sex-reassignment surgery is rarely available in Pakistan, and the 2018 Act's healthcare non-discrimination clause is routinely not honoured in practice.

Open expression carries personal risk. Pakistani media censor LGBTQ-related news: the government blocked Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times left a blank space where a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this, banning 'obscene' publications and public acts and designating an assembly of five or more persons an unlawful assembly where the common object is to commit any offence, so public gathering carries legal exposure as well as risk from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups.

No legal recognition exists for same-sex partnerships. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, Article 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and Article 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council; Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore, Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat, declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, but that declaration has no civil effect and the Federal Shariat Court's 2023 ruling cuts the other way.
tangentialFactors:
Consensual same-sex acts remain criminalised under section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code, carrying two years to life imprisonment; the definition is unclear and, per Human Dignity Trust as of December 2024, only men are criminalised. The UK Home Office assesses that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution, an assessment that concerns state action rather than the risk of violence from non-state actors, which is separately documented.

The constitutional framework itself constrains protection: Article 227 requires all laws to conform to Islam as advised by a government-appointed Islamic council, the mechanism under which the Federal Shariat Court reviewed the 2018 Act. This places any trans-specific statutory protection in the country permanently within a review that other jurisdictions do not face.

Estimates of the transgender population run to around 500,000 citizens facing social exclusion and abuse, a figure cited in September 2025 reporting. For comparison, the country's progressive 2018 statute is frequently described in regional coverage as a legislative turning point, and The Diplomat's July 2025 assessment frames citizens as legally recognised yet socially forsaken.

HIV and sexual-health data form an adjacent background risk: the epidemic began in 1987, government estimates from 2004 put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV while critics suggest 70,000 to 80,000 and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000, and a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk with poor access to condoms and little public health education. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records same-sex conduct as criminalised, societal violence and discrimination, and harassment and violence against transgender persons known locally as khwaja sira.
localsOnly:
Residents live with the statutory framework daily: the 2018 Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, and the 2020 Rules allow an 'X' marker on administrative documents, yet local reporting documents denial of basic education and healthcare to transgender people notwithstanding those clauses.

Sex-reassignment surgery is rarely available in Pakistan because of cost, limited training and social taboos, so many transgender women obtain hormones and silicone injections through unregulated providers without proper equipment or supervision. Post-operative and emergency care is unreliable, as the 2016 Peshawar case shows.

Local organising exists within limits: a small clerical body in Lahore declared transgender marriages valid under Islamic law in June 2016, and the LGBTQ community can socialise, organise and date, in rare cases living together as couples, but almost always in secret. Openly LGBTQ Pakistanis face forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail and violence from family and community, and a 2005 tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death.

Pakistani media suppress LGBTQ-related coverage, and press outlets self-censor: the Express Tribune left a blank space rather than print a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story. Local activists named in press reports have requested anonymity or had identifying details withheld for their security.

The 2010 Supreme Court order directing free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people remains the operative affirmative mandate alongside the 2018 Act, but both are implemented unevenly by provincial authorities and hospitals.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 'X' marker issued under the 2020 Rules is accepted at international border posts, by airlines, or by foreign missions issuing visas is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved here. No information is available on airport or immigration screening practices that could disclose a trans visitor's status on arrival.

The current status of the appeals against the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 ruling is not sourced beyond the November 2025 UK Home Office note describing ongoing legal disputes. Which sections of the 2018 Act are operative in practice, as distinct from on the statute book, is not resolved by these sources.

No source in the inventory addresses whether Pakistan has hate-crime sentencing enhancement covering gender identity, or any complaints mechanism available to a foreign national. Reporting requirements for trans visitors are likewise not sourced.

The precise scope of section 377 as applied, and whether a trans woman's relationships are assessed under it by sex assigned at birth or by recognised gender, is described in the sources as unclear.
